N3.claim: Under cumulative bans B_k = first k of [BFS, DFS, IDDFS, A*, greedy] on Qwen3-32B thinking, mechanistic compliance falls with k while lexical compliance stays high.
criteria: k=1: lexical and mechanistic compliance both >= 0.7

CONFIRMATION: held-out k=5 (W4/W5/P6/P7) gap >= 0.4 with Newcombe lower bound > 0

sensitivities: fine classes (e.g. greedy at k=4 is compliant)

N1.claim: Across the 10 retraced five-name-ban configurations, lexical compliance exceeds mechanistic compliance (gap = lex - mech, among traceable programs).

examples.input: **The alias test.** The audit computed, on CPU from iteration 8's stored states and geodesics, how the geodesic distance g of each non-banned alias to the banned five relates to the number of content words the alias shares with a banned alias. Its four gates passed; the last recomputed the k-nearest-neighbour geodesics independently from the stored states and matched the stored k = 15 matrix at Spearman 1.000. Across the 15 aliases, g falls as overlap rises (Spearman -0.61 at k 15, exact p 0.0093 over 360,360 assignments; -0.77 at k 10, p 0.0007). Within algorithms the relation vanishes: the stratified test, which permutes overlap only among the three aliases of one algorithm, gives -0.12 (p 0.46 over 216 effective relabelings), and the slope of a fixed-effects fit has the wrong sign (+2.36, p 0.78). With only five algorithm centroids, the centroid-level Spearman of -0.63 cannot reach significance (p 0.133; the attainable floor is 0.033). The committed reading is that g follows alias overlap across algorithms, but the pattern is carried by algorithm identity: on this manifold names and mechanisms are confounded. A sensitivity on the model's own BPE tokens gives a borderline within-algorithm statistic (-0.50, p 0.057; -0.40, p 0.11 at k 10), so a small name effect inside algorithms is not excluded. The placebos fail as required and a planted name effect is recovered (Table 424). The figure of Section 8.8 plots the alias-level points and the classical MDS of the stored k = 15 geodesics.

Across the 15 aliases, g falls as overlap rises (Spearman -0.61 at k 15, exact p 0.0093 over 360,360 assignments; -0.77 at k 10, p 0.0007). Within algorithms the relation is not detected (three algorithms; underpowered) (iteration-10 correction): the stratified test, which permutes overlap only among the three aliases of one algorithm, gives -0.12 (p 0.46 over 216 effective relabelings), and the slope of a fixed-effects fit has the wrong sign (+2.36, p 0.78). With only five algorithm centroids, the centroid-level Spearman of -0.63 cannot reach significance (p 0.133; the attainable floor is 0.033). The committed reading is that g follows alias overlap across algorithms, but the pattern is carried by algorithm identity: on this manifold names and mechanisms are confounded. A sensitivity on the model's own BPE tokens gives a borderline within-algorithm statistic (-0.50, p 0.057; -0.40, p 0.11 at k 10), so a small name effect inside algorithms is not excluded. The placebos fail as required and a planted name effect is recovered (Table 424). The figure of Section 8.8 plots the alias-level points and the classical MDS of the stored k = 15 geodesics.

examples.input: **The exhaustion curve.** Cumulative bans of the first k names in Qwen3-32B's frequency order (BFS; then DFS, IDDFS, A* and greedy best-first) were sampled 50 times per k on three templates, with the full ban also sampled on four held-out templates, for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-14B with thinking (Table 431 and the figure below). At k = 1 both models comply by name and by mechanism in every completed program: banning BFS changes the mechanism. Lexical compliance stays at or above 0.86 at every k on the committed templates. Mechanistic compliance by the runtime label falls with k, from 1.00 to 0.22 for Qwen3-32B and from 1.00 to 0.10 for Qwen3-14B (Jonckheere-Terpstra [149] Monte-Carlo p 0.00001 for each model; Cochran-Armitage [150] one-sided p below 0.00001). At k = 5 the gap is 0.67 (0.50 to 0.78) and 0.76 (0.59 to 0.85), and on the held-out templates 0.56 and 0.68. Every committed criterion is met, but descriptively. The tracer's curve falls less and is not monotone for Qwen3-32B (1.00, 0.86, 0.91, 0.47, 0.67), because it reads the coordinate-key heaps and Bellman-Ford rounds of the late cells as compliant. Correctness does not follow compliance: at k = 1 only 9 of 50 Qwen3-32B programs and 14 of 50 Qwen3-14B programs pass the hidden tests, against 33 to 40 and 17 to 27 of 50 at the larger k.
examples.output: **The exhaustion curve.** Cumulative bans of the first k names in Qwen3-32B's frequency order (BFS; then DFS, IDDFS, A* and greedy best-first) were sampled 50 times per k on three templates, with the full ban also sampled on four held-out templates, for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-14B with thinking (Table 431 and the figure below). At k = 1 both models comply by name and by mechanism in every completed program: banning BFS changes the mechanism. Lexical compliance stays at or above 0.86 at every k on the committed templates. At k = 5 the gap is 0.67 (0.50 to 0.78) and 0.76 (0.59 to 0.85), and on the held-out templates 0.56 and 0.68. Whether the committed bars are met depends on the reading (iteration-10 correction). By the runtime label both models meet every committed criterion, descriptively. The registered fine-class sensitivity was a no-op for the runtime label in the executed code: results/n3.json repeats the primary in all 12 cells, because analysis_v9.py applies fine classes only when the mechanism field is the tracer's; it was applied for the tracer (results/n3_tracer.json). Computed for the runtime label, it changes one step: from k = 3 to k = 4 Qwen3-32B falls from 0.84 to 0.24 by the coarse runtime label, but 11 of the 35 coarse violations at k = 4 are greedy best-first programs, a name not yet banned, and with fine classes compliance is 22 of 46 = 0.48 (tracer 0.47 coarse and 0.82 fine); at k = 5 the fine runtime value equals the coarse one (10 of 46 = 0.22). By the runtime label mechanistic compliance falls to 0.22 (Qwen3-32B) and 0.10 (Qwen3-14B) at five names; by hand reads to 0.59 and 0.12; by the tracer to 0.67 and 0.24 (fine classes 0.74 and 0.37; Table 431b). Qwen3-14B meets the k = 5 bar of a 0.4 gap under every reading (runtime label 0.76, hand reads 0.73, tracer 0.61, tracer fine 0.49) and the held-out bar under every reading except the tracer's fine classes, where its held-out gap is 0.38 (lexical 0.78 against 20 of 50 = 0.40). Qwen3-32B meets both bars only by the runtime label (0.67 at k = 5, 0.56 held out): at k = 5 the hand reads (0.30), the coarse tracer (0.22) and the fine tracer (0.15) fall below 0.4, and on the held-out templates the hand reads give 0.396, just below the bar, and the coarse tracer 0.42; counting unit-weight Dijkstra, IDA* and jump point search as compliant gives 0.57 at k = 5 and 0.31 held out. Its tracer curve is not monotone (1.00, 0.86, 0.91, 0.47, 0.67), because the tracer reads the coordinate-key heaps and Bellman-Ford rounds of the late cells as compliant. The hand reads adjudicate between the instruments on exactly these programs: they agree with the tracer on 0.88 of the 76 read programs and with the runtime label on 0.64; coordinate-key heaps and grid Bellman-Ford rounds are other known disciplines, and the runtime label reads the Bellman-Ford rounds as iterative deepening. Correctness does not follow compliance: at k = 1 only 9 of 50 Qwen3-32B programs and 14 of 50 Qwen3-14B programs pass the hidden tests, against 33 to 40 and 17 to 27 of 50 at the larger k.
